newsitem.title: UK: Bankers, academics line up for British policy squad.
newsitem.headline: Bankers, academics line up for British policy squad.

text.p: Britain's new Labour government is expected to cement its newly won reputation for economic rectitude by appointing a quintet of bankers, academics and business executives to its planned nine-member monetary policy committee.

Gavyn Davies, chief economist at investment bank Goldman Sachs, is the hot favourite to fill the new position of second deputy governor of the Bank of England. Indeed some financial experts believe the role has been designed especially for him.

"My guess is there will be one economist with city and labour party links -- that's Gavyn Davies -- one from industry, one from the regions and one right-winger to keep it ecumenical," one leading left-wing economist said.

Multi-millionaire Davies was a member of the previous Conservative government's panel of independent advisers and has been a Labour adviser since the last Labour government in the 1970s. His wife, Sue Nye is head of Brown's office.

The chief contenders for the other four positions include Bridget Rosewell, executive chair of Business Strategies Ltd and another member of the now defunct treasury advisory panel; Charles Goodhart of the London School of Economics Centre for Economic performance (CEP) and Richard Layard, the CEP's head.
Underlining Labour's rejection of traditional Socialist dogma in favour of more market-friendly economics, there is unlikely to be a single trade unionist in the line-up.
"Appointing anyone from a trades union would be a very bad sign indeed and it's not a mistake the government is going to make," one senior business source and ex-Treasury official said.
"They're going to play safe and they'll stick to people who understand monetary policy."

Finance Minister Gordon Brown delighted financial markets on Tuesday by announcing he was handing over conduct of monetary policy to the Bank of England in a bid to remove political bias from interest rate decisions.

The five government appointees on the new committee, which will set interest rates, are likely to have a left-wing bias but will be carefully selected so that the new regime's anti-inflation credentials remain intact.

The new committee -- which will have a total of nine members -- will also include central Bank governor and anti-inflation Hawk Eddie George, deputy governor Howard Davies, a new deputy governor and two executive directors -- likely to be Mervyn King, the bank's economic expert and market specialist Ian Plenderleith.
Among the favourites for the four other posts to be chosen by the Treasury, Rosewell is renowned for her expertise on what is happening to the economy at a regional level.

"They have to get the whole span of thought," said one former treasury official. "Bridget Rosewell is really very good on the regional side. She's an excellent economist with extemely good business contacts -- she'll stir these guys up."
Prime Minister Tony Blair has already made history by appointing the highest ever number of women ministers and experts doubt that the final committee line-up will be exclusively male.
"But if it's Bridget Rosewell, it's certainly not going to be a token woman," the former official said.
City economists who have previously worked at the Bank of England or the Treasury say Layard, another millionaire, has particular expertise on the labour market.
His colleague Goodhart is seen as less overtly political and ex-Bank of England officials say he would bring a strong academic reputation.

Others mooted for the positions are Citibank chief economist Neil McKinnon, who has also been a Labour adviser, and Flemings economist Peter Warburton, although he was an adviser of former Conservative finance minister Norman Lamont.

Also in the running are former treasury panel members or "wise men" Martin Weale, director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research, and David Currie, now a Labour member of the House of Lords.
Gerry Holtham of the left wing Institute for Public Policy Research is also a possiblity as is Oxford University academic Andrew Graham.
There is as yet no indication when the new appointments will be made or indeed whether the positions will be full or part-time.
